entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18352"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Heb.3.1-Heb.3.19">He 3:1-19</reference>. The Son of God Greater than Moses, Wherefore Unbelief towards Him Will Incur a Heavier Punishment than Befell Unbelieving Israel in the Wilderness.</title> <div sID="gen38298" type="x-p"/> As Moses especially was the prophet by whom "God in times past spake to the fathers," being the mediator of the law, Paul deems it necessary now to show that, great as was Moses, the Son of God is greater. Ebrard in Alford remarks, The angel of the covenant came in the name of God before Israel; Moses in the name of Israel before God; whereas the high priest came both in the name of God (bearing the name Jehovah on his forehead) before Israel, and in the name of Israel (bearing the names of the twelve tribes on his breast) before God (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.9-Exod.29.36">Ex 28:9-29, 36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">38</reference>). Now Christ is above the angels, according to the first and second chapters because (1) as Son of God He is higher; and (2) because manhood, though originally lower than angels, is in Him exalted above them to the lordship of "the world to come," inasmuch as He is at once Messenger of God to men, and also atoning Priest-Representative of men before God (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">He 2:17</reference>, 18). Parallel with this line of argument as to His superiority to angels (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">He 1:4</reference>) runs that which here follows as to His superiority to Moses (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">He 3:3</reference>): (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1</reference>) because as Son over the house; He is above the servant in the house (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.5">He 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">6</reference>), just as the angels were shown to be but ministering (serving) spirits (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">He 1:14</reference>), whereas He is the Son (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.7">He 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.8">8</reference>); (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>) because the bringing of Israel into the promised rest, which was not finished by Moses, is accomplished by Him (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.1-Heb.4.11">He 4:1-11</reference>), through His being not merely a leader and lawgiver as Moses, but also a propitiatory High Priest (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.14">He 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.10">5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen38298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18352"/><hi type="bold">1. Wherefore--</hi>Greek, "Whence," that is, seeing we have such a sympathizing Helper you ought to "consider attentively," "contemplate"; fix your eyes and mind on Him with a view to profiting by the contemplation (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">He 12:2</reference>). The Greek word is often used by Luke, Paul's companion (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.24">Lu 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen38299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brethren--</hi>in Christ, the common bond of union.<div eID="gen38300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">partakers--</hi>"of the Holy Ghost."<div eID="gen38301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavenly calling--</hi>coming to us from heaven, and leading us to heaven whence it comes. <reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">Php 3:14</reference>, "the high calling"; Greek "the calling above," that is, heavenly.<div eID="gen38302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Apostle and High Priest of our profession--</hi>There is but one Greek article to both nouns, "Him who is at once Apostle and High Priest"--Apostle, as Ambassador (a higher designation than "angel"-messenger) sent by the Father (<reference osisRef="John.20.21">Joh 20:21</reference>), pleading the cause of God with us; High Priest, as pleading our cause with God. Both His Apostleship and High Priesthood are comprehended in the one title, Mediator [Bengel]. Though the title "Apostle" is nowhere else applied to Christ, it is appropriate here in addressing Hebrews, who used the term of the delegates sent by the high priest to collect the temple tribute from Jews resident in foreign countries, even as Christ was Delegate of the Father to this world far off from Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.37">Mt 21:37</reference>). Hence as what applies to Him, applies also to His people, the Twelve are designated His apostles, even as He is the Father's (<reference osisRef="John.20.21">Joh 20:21</reference>). It was desirable to avoid designating Him here "angel," in order to distinguish His nature from that of angels mentioned before, though he is "the Angel of the Covenant." The "legate of the Church" (Sheliach Tsibbur) offered up the prayers in the synagogue in the name of all, and for all. So Jesus, "the Apostle of our profession," is delegated to intercede for the Church before the Father. The words "of our profession," mark that it is not of the legal ritual, but of our Christian faith, that He is the High Priest. Paul compares Him as an Apostle to Moses; as High Priest to Aaron. He alone holds both offices combined, and in a more eminent degree than either, which those two brothers held apart.<div eID="gen38303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profession--</hi>"confession," corresponds to God having spoken to us by His Son, sent as Apostle and High Priest. What God proclaims we confess. <div eID="gen38304" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 3 He 3:1-19. The Son of God Greater than Moses, Wherefore Unbelief towards Him Will Incur a Heavier Punishment than Befell Unbelieving Israel in the Wilderness. Parallel with this line of argument as to His superiority to angels (He 1:4) runs that which here follows as to His superiority to Moses (He 3:3): (1) because as Son over the house; He is above the servant in the house (He 3:5, 6), just as the angels were shown to be but ministering (serving) spirits (He 1:14), whereas He is the Son (He 3:7, 8); (2) because the bringing of Israel into the promised rest, which was not finished by Moses, is accomplished by Him (He 4:1-11), through His being not merely a leader and lawgiver as Moses, but also a propitiatory High Priest (He 4:14; 5:10). 1. Wherefore--Greek, "Whence," that is, seeing we have such a sympathizing Helper you ought to "consider attentively," "contemplate"; fix your eyes and mind on Him with a view to profiting by the contemplation (He 12:2). The Greek word is often used by Luke, Paul's companion (Lu 12:24, 27). brethren--in Christ, the common bond of union. partakers--"of the Holy Ghost." heavenly calling--coming to us from heaven, and leading us to heaven whence it comes. Though the title "Apostle" is nowhere else applied to Christ, it is appropriate here in addressing Hebrews, who used the term of the delegates sent by the high priest to collect the temple tribute from Jews resident in foreign countries, even as Christ was Delegate of the Father to this world far off from Him (Mt 21:37). Hence as what applies to Him, applies also to His people, the Twelve are designated His apostles, even as He is the Father's (Joh 20:21). It was desirable to avoid designating Him here "angel," in order to distinguish His nature from that of angels mentioned before, though he is "the Angel of the Covenant." The "legate of the Church" (Sheliach Tsibbur) offered up the prayers in the synagogue in the name of all, and for all. The words "of our profession," mark that it is not of the legal ritual, but of our Christian faith, that He is the High Priest. Paul compares Him as an Apostle to Moses; as High Priest to Aaron. He alone holds both offices combined, and in a more eminent degree than either, which those two brothers held apart. profession--"confession," corresponds to God having spoken to us by His Son, sent as Apostle and High Priest. What God proclaims we confess.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18353"/><div sID="gen38305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18353"/>2. He first notes the feature of resemblance between Moses and Christ, in order to conciliate the Hebrew Christians whom He addressed, and who still entertained a very high opinion of Moses; he afterwards brings forward Christ's superiority to Moses.<div eID="gen38305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Who was faithful--</hi>The Greek implies also that He still is faithful, namely, as our mediating High Priest, faithful to the trust God has assigned Him (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">He 2:17</reference>). So Moses in God's house (<reference osisRef="Num.12.7">Nu 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen38306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed him--</hi>"made Him" High Priest; to be supplied from the preceding context. Greek, "made"; so in <reference osisRef="Heb.5.5">He 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.6">1Sa 12:6</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Ac 2:36</reference>; so the Greek fathers. Not as Alford, with Ambrose and the Latins, "created Him," that is, as man, in His incarnation. The likeness of Moses to Messiah was foretold by Moses himself (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>). Other prophets only explained Moses, who was in this respect superior to them; but Christ was like Moses, yet superior. <div eID="gen38307" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18354"/><div sID="gen38308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18354"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>assigning the reason why they should "consider" attentively "Christ" (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">He 3:1</reference>), highly as they regard Moses who resembled Him in faithfulness (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">He 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen38308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was--</hi>Greek, "has been."<div eID="gen38309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counted worthy of more glory--</hi>by God, when He exalted Him to His own right hand. The Hebrew Christians admitted the fact (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.13">He 1:13</reference>).<div eID="gen38310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">builded the house--</hi>Greek, "inasmuch as He hath more honor than the house, who prepared it," or "established it" [Alford]. The Greek verb is used purposely instead of "builded," in order to mark that the building meant is not a literal, but a spiritual house: the Church both of the Old Testament and New Testament; and that the building of such a house includes all the preparations of providence and grace needed to furnish it with "living stones" and fitting "servants." Thus, as Christ the Founder and Establisher (in Old Testament as well as the New Testament) is greater than the house so established, including the servants, He is greater also than Moses, who was but a "servant." Moses, as a servant, is a portion of the house, and less than the house; Christ, as the Instrumental Creator of all things, must be God, and so greater than the house of which Moses was but a part. Glory is the result of honor. <div eID="gen38311" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18367"/><div sID="gen38362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18367"/><hi type="bold">16. For some--</hi>rather interrogatively, "For WHO was it that, when they had heard (referring to 'if ye will hear,' <reference osisRef="Heb.3.15">He 3:15</reference>), did provoke (God)?" The "For" implies, Ye need to take heed against unbelief: for, was it not because of unbelief that all our fathers were excluded (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.3">Eze 2:3</reference>)? "Some," and "not all," would be a faint way of putting his argument, when his object is to show the universality of the evil. Not merely some, but all the Israelites, for the solitary exceptions, Joshua and Caleb, are hardly to be taken into account in so general a statement. So <reference osisRef="Heb.3.17">He 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.18">18</reference>, are interrogative: (1) the beginning of the provocation, soon after the departure from Egypt, is marked in <reference osisRef="Heb.3.16">He 3:16</reference>; (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>) the forty years of it in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.17">He 3:17</reference>; (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">3</reference>) the denial of entrance into the land of rest, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.18">He 3:18</reference>. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.5">1Co 10:5</reference>, "with the majority of them God was displeased."<div eID="gen38362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">howbeit--</hi>"Nay (why need I put the question?), was it not all that came out of Egypt?" (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.1">Ex 17:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen38363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Moses--</hi>by the instrumentality of Moses as their leader. <div eID="gen38364" type="x-p"/>
